case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act authorizes suits against Cuban state-owned entities for “trafficking” in expropriated property without requiring plaintiffs to satisfy an exception to foreign sovereign immunity under the FSIA.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms‑Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. §§ 6081–6085, in relation to the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611 (especially the baseline immunity rule and exceptions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Exxon Mobil argues that Title III’s cause of action and jurisdictional language reflect Congress’s intent to make Cuban agencies and instrumentalities (including state-owned entities that hold/operate expropriated assets) suable for trafficking, notwithstanding the FSIA’s presumptive immunity. Exxon (supported by the United States and business amici) contends that requiring Title III plaintiffs to separately plead and prove an FSIA exception would undermine the Helms‑Burton Act’s core purpose—creating an effective damages remedy and deterrent for continued exploitation of confiscated U.S. property—and would make many Title III suits functionally impossible given how hard it can be to fit trafficking claims into FSIA’s existing exceptions (e.g., commercial-activity or expropriation-related pathways).
case_analysis.respondent_position: CIMEX and co-respondents argue that the FSIA supplies the exclusive rules for when foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities may be sued in U.S. courts, and Title III does not clearly and explicitly displace that immunity framework. In their view, Title III may create a substantive liability rule (and a private right of action), but it does not itself constitute an FSIA immunity exception; therefore, plaintiffs must still establish jurisdiction by fitting within an FSIA exception. Respondents (supported by foreign sovereign immunity and international law scholars) emphasize the strong clear-statement requirement for stripping sovereign immunity, the foreign-relations consequences of implying an unstated exception, and comparative/international practice recognizing that suits effectively challenging Cuba’s expropriations can amount to indirect impleader of the sovereign and thus trigger immunity concerns unless immunity is expressly lifted.
key_precedents: Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria
Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp.
Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran
Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela v. Helmerich & Payne Int’l Drilling Co.

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—that Title III defines “person” to include certain governmental entities and sets out liability for “trafficking,” plus its own jurisdiction/venue provisions—still does not amount to the unmistakable immunity-stripping statement required to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, that is liability-facing text, and Amerada Hess makes the FSIA the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state absent clear congressional displacement; Rubin reinforces that we do not infer FSIA carveouts from general remedial purpose or definitional breadth. Justice Sotomayor’s statutory-coherence and foreign-relations concerns underscore why a narrow holding is available and appropriate: Title III supplies a cause of action, but plaintiffs must still establish an existing FSIA exception to get through the jurisdictional gateway. Nothing raised in conference undermines that minimal, precedent-centered resolution.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest argument—that Title III’s definition of “person” and its broad trafficking liability necessarily contemplate suits against Cuban instrumentalities—still does not supply the kind of unmistakable immunity-stripping text required to displace the FSIA’s command that a “foreign state shall be immune” absent an enumerated exception. As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, liability-facing language and even general jurisdiction/venue provisions cannot override the FSIA’s comprehensive, exclusive jurisdictional scheme recognized in Amerada Hess, and Rubin reinforces that we do not infer FSIA carveouts by implication. The better textual reconciliation is that Title III creates substantive liability that may be enforced only when an existing FSIA exception independently opens the courthouse door, rather than silently amending §§ 1604–1605. Because Title III does not expressly add an FSIA exception or state it applies “notwithstanding” the FSIA, I see no basis, consistent with original meaning and statutory text, to treat it as an implied abrogation of sovereign immunity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that Title III defines “person” broadly and creates a federal cause of action with its own jurisdiction/venue provisions, arguably signaling Congress meant to reach state-owned Cuban entities; but under Amerada Hess, a cause of action and general jurisdictional language are not enough to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive immunity-and-jurisdiction scheme without an unmistakable statement. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on the FSIA as the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” reinforces that § 1330(a) and the FSIA exceptions remain gatekeepers even when Congress creates new substantive liability rules. Rubin underscores the same clear-statement demand when litigants seek to alter FSIA protections by implication rather than express amendment. Given the practical foreign-relations consequences of implying an immunity override for Cuban instrumentalities, I see no legal basis to infer an unstated FSIA exception from Title III’s silence on immunity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that Title III’s definition of “person” and its broad trafficking liability seem designed to reach state-owned Cuban actors, but that is still liability language, not the unmistakable immunity/jurisdiction instruction needed to override the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Amerada Hess—that FSIA is the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over foreign states—reinforces my pragmatic concern that treating Title III as an implied FSIA exception would turn sovereign immunity into an unstable, litigation-by-implication inquiry with significant foreign-relations spillover. Justice Kagan’s statutory-coherence point is persuasive: Title III can operate fully as a cause of action while still requiring plaintiffs to clear the FSIA gateway, and Rubin’s insistence on explicit authorization cautions against inferring immunity-stripping from silence. Absent a clear statement amending §§ 1604–1605 or adding a new exception, plaintiffs must proceed (if at all) under existing FSIA exceptions rather than a freestanding Title III workaround.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the textual breadth of Title III—its cause of action against any “person,” including certain governmental entities, plus its own jurisdiction/venue provisions—which is awkward if the primary targets are immune. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Amerada Hess treats the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state, and Title III’s liability and venue language is not an unmistakable immunity-stripping or FSIA-amending instruction. Justice Barrett’s observation underscores why a pragmatic textualist cannot infer an FSIA carveout here: Congress routinely uses “notwithstanding” clauses or adds a § 1605 exception when it means to alter immunity, and Rubin cautions against deriving immunity changes from general remedial design. Statutory coherence is preserved by reading Title III to supply substantive liability while leaving the FSIA to supply the jurisdictional gateway through its enumerated exceptions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The opposing side’s best textual point is that Title III defines “person” to include certain governmental entities and contains its own cause-of-action and jurisdiction/venue provisions, suggesting Congress anticipated suits against state-linked actors. But as Justice Kagan rightly frames it, that is liability-facing language and cannot do the separate work—required by Amerada Hess and reinforced by Rubin—of unmistakably stripping FSIA immunity or adding a new § 1605 exception. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state is decisive for me: absent an express amendment or a “notwithstanding FSIA” directive, we should not infer an immunity abrogation from statutory breadth or remedial purpose, especially given the separation-of-powers and foreign-relations stakes. Title III can operate coherently as a cause of action only where an existing FSIA exception independently opens the courthouse doors.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—that Title III’s definition of “person,” paired with a cause of action and its own jurisdiction/venue provisions, implies Congress meant to permit suits against Cuban instrumentalities—still falls short of the unmistakable immunity-stripping statement our FSIA cases require. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Amerada Hess is decisive for me: the FSIA is the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state, and Title III’s liability-facing language does not amend §§ 1604–1605 or add an exception in the way Congress knows how to do. Justice Kagan’s statutory-coherence point reinforces the institutional and practical concern that we should not infer a major foreign-relations-sensitive immunity carveout from definitional breadth and remedial purpose, especially after Rubin’s insistence on explicit authorization when altering FSIA protections. Title III can operate fully as a substantive liability rule for defendants already within an FSIA exception, without silently displacing the FSIA’s comprehensive gatekeeping framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Title III authorizes suit against any “person,” and defines that term broadly enough to encompass some governmental entities, suggesting Congress contemplated suits against Cuban instrumentalities. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Amerada Hess treats the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state, and Title III’s liability-facing language plus general jurisdiction/venue provisions do not amount to the unmistakable immunity-stripping statement needed to displace §§ 1604–1605. Justice Kagan’s statutory-coherence point reinforces the textual reading that the statutes can operate in tandem: Title III supplies a cause of action, while FSIA exceptions remain the gateway to haling a foreign state (or its agencies/instrumentalities) into court. Rubin’s insistence on clear authorization in the FSIA context further undercuts any inference of implied abrogation from silence, particularly given the foreign-relations consequences Congress would be expected to address expressly.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Title III’s definition of “person,” plus its cause of action and jurisdiction/venue provisions, presupposes suits against Cuban instrumentalities; but as Justice Kagan emphasizes, that is liability-facing drafting and does not amount to an unmistakable immunity abrogation. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Amerada Hess—that the FSIA is the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state—fits my procedural-fairness and rule-of-law concerns: we should not convert immunity into a guesswork inquiry based on remedial purpose when Congress has provided a comprehensive gateway in §§ 1604–1605. Rubin, invoked by several colleagues, reinforces that we do not infer FSIA displacement from general statutory language, especially given predictable foreign-relations consequences that Congress would be expected to address expressly. Title III can operate pragmatically as a substantive liability rule only where an existing FSIA exception independently opens the courthouse door; absent clearer text, I do not see a legally sound basis to treat it as a standalone FSIA override.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” in U.S. courts, and Congress must speak clearly if it intends to abrogate that immunity regime. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434, 439 (1989). Title III of Helms‑Burton creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not unmistakably state that Cuban agencies or instrumentalities may be sued notwithstanding the FSIA’s baseline immunity, nor does it expressly add a new § 1605 exception. Consistent with Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran and this Court’s reluctance to infer implied waivers or unstated immunity carveouts, plaintiffs must still satisfy an FSIA exception for jurisdiction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA’s text provides the baseline rule that a “foreign state shall be immune” unless a statutory exception applies, and it supplies the jurisdictional grant for such suits in § 1330; absent a clear textual displacement, that framework controls. This Court has repeatedly described the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over foreign states in federal court, rejecting reliance on other jurisdictional statutes like § 1331. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434–39 (1989). Title III creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not expressly add an FSIA immunity exception or unmistakably abrogate the immunity of Cuban agencies and instrumentalities; under a textualist approach, courts may not infer an unstated abrogation with significant foreign-relations consequences. See Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran, 584 U.S. ___ (2018) (requiring clear statutory authorization when altering FSIA immunity/related rules).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole and exclusive standards” for jurisdiction and immunity in suits against a foreign state or its agencies and instrumentalities, so a Title III plaintiff must establish an applicable FSIA exception to proceed in federal court. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp. holds that § 1330(a) displaces other jurisdictional grants (including § 1331) and that courts may not infer alternative routes around the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme absent a clear statement. Title III (22 U.S.C. §§ 6081–6085) creates a cause of action and liability rule for “trafficking,” but it does not clearly and expressly abrogate sovereign immunity or add an FSIA exception, and this Court has required that kind of explicit congressional instruction when immunity is to be stripped (see also Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran). Practical and foreign-relations consequences reinforce adhering to the FSIA framework rather than implying an unstated immunity override for Cuban state-owned entities.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FSIA provides the “sole and exclusive standards” for subject-matter jurisdiction and immunity in suits against foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities, and § 1330(a) displaces other jurisdictional grants. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 437–39 (1989); see also Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488–89 (1983). Title III creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not clearly and explicitly abrogate foreign sovereign immunity or enact an FSIA exception, and this Court has required a clear statement before treating later statutes as displacing FSIA’s framework. Given the significant foreign-relations consequences and the statute’s silence on immunity, plaintiffs must proceed (if at all) by fitting their claims within an existing FSIA exception (e.g., commercial activity).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the baseline rule and the exclusive set of exceptions for exercising jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, and this Court has repeatedly described it as the “sole basis” for such jurisdiction. See Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434 (1989); see also Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran (reaffirming the need for clear statutory authorization when limiting FSIA protections). Title III creates a cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” and defines “person” to include certain governmental entities, 22 U.S.C. §§ 6023(11), 6082(a)(1), but it nowhere speaks in clear, jurisdictional terms to displace FSIA immunity or to create a new FSIA exception; absent that clear statement, workably and coherently, courts should require plaintiffs to proceed through an FSIA exception (e.g., § 1605(a)(2) or § 1605(a)(3)). That approach preserves statutory coherence between Helms‑Burton and the FSIA while avoiding the foreign-relations consequences of implying an unstated immunity abrogation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA provides the baseline and generally exclusive rules for when a foreign state or its agencies/instrumentalities may be haled into U.S. court, and this Court has held it is “the sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” absent a clearly expressed statutory displacement. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 439 (1989). Title III of Helms‑Burton creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but nothing in 22 U.S.C. §§ 6081–6085 unmistakably states that Cuban state-owned entities may be sued notwithstanding FSIA immunity or that Title III itself operates as an FSIA exception. Consistent with Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran and related clear-statement cases, courts should not infer abrogation of sovereign immunity from general jurisdictional or liability language; plaintiffs must still satisfy an FSIA exception under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1605–1607.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FSIA establishes the “sole basis” for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities in U.S. courts, and displacement of that immunity regime requires a clear statement from Congress. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp. and later decisions (including Rubin) underscore that courts should not infer new immunity exceptions from general causes of action or policy aims absent express jurisdictional or immunity-stripping language. Title III of Helms‑Burton creates a private right of action for “trafficking,” but it does not expressly abrogate sovereign immunity or amend 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604–1607, so plaintiffs must still satisfy an FSIA exception to proceed. Reading Title III to impliedly override the FSIA would be inconsistent with the FSIA’s comprehensive framework and would risk significant foreign-relations consequences that Congress has not clearly authorized.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSIA’s text makes foreign states and their agencies or instrumentalities “immune from the jurisdiction” of U.S. courts unless a statutory exception applies, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604–1605, and this Court has repeatedly treated the FSIA as supplying the governing jurisdictional framework for suits against foreign sovereigns. In Amerada Hess, we emphasized that the FSIA is the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” in federal court, and in cases like Rubin we have required clear statutory authorization before allowing litigation that would circumvent the FSIA’s immunity rules. Title III creates a cause of action for “trafficking” in confiscated property and contains jurisdiction/venue provisions, but it does not expressly amend the FSIA or create a new immunity exception applicable to “foreign states” as defined in § 1603. Absent a clear statement displacing FSIA immunity, methodological consistency and the FSIA’s comprehensive structure require plaintiffs to proceed (if at all) by satisfying an existing FSIA exception.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FSIA establishes a comprehensive, exclusive framework for when foreign states and their agencies or instrumentalities may be sued in U.S. courts, and subject-matter jurisdiction exists only through 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a) when an FSIA exception applies. Under Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., Congress displaced other jurisdictional grants (including § 1331) and set “the sole and exclusive standards” for adjudicating immunity and jurisdiction, so a separate statute must contain a clear statement if it is to abrogate immunity. Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act (22 U.S.C. §§ 6081–6085) creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not clearly and explicitly create a new FSIA immunity exception or otherwise override 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604–1605. Given the foreign-relations stakes and the Court’s insistence on clear statutory direction in immunity and related contexts (e.g., Rubin; Altmann), plaintiffs must still satisfy an FSIA exception to proceed against Cuban state-owned entities.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act (Helms-Burton) authorizes U.S. courts to hear trafficking claims against Cuban state agencies/instrumentalities without requiring plaintiffs to satisfy an exception to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms-Burton), 22 U.S.C. § 6021 et seq. (creating a civil damages cause of action for trafficking in property confiscated by the Cuban government), and the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602 et seq. (presumptive immunity and exceptions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Exxon Mobil argues that Congress enacted Title III to create an effective U.S. damages remedy for victims of Cuba’s unlawful expropriations and for subsequent “trafficking” in confiscated property, and that this purpose would be undermined if Cuban agencies and instrumentalities could invoke FSIA immunity unless plaintiffs can fit within a narrow FSIA exception. Petitioner, supported by the United States and business amici, contends that Title III should be read to permit suits against Cuban instrumentalities (often the entities actually holding/using the expropriated assets) without separately pleading and proving an FSIA exception, because Congress intended Title III to function as a targeted accountability mechanism and compensation scheme for U.S. claimants whose property was taken and then commercialized through state-controlled entities.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Corporación Cimex and the other respondents argue that the FSIA provides the exclusive and presumptive immunity framework for foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities in U.S. courts, and that Title III does not clearly and expressly displace that framework. In their view, Title III creates a cause of action but does not itself strip immunity; therefore, a Title III plaintiff must still establish jurisdiction by fitting the case within an FSIA exception. Respondents and scholar amici emphasize separation-of-powers and foreign-relations concerns, the strong presumption that immunity rules are controlled by the FSIA absent unmistakable congressional direction, and comparative/international-law considerations (including foreign court practice resisting suits that effectively adjudicate the legality of Cuba’s sovereign expropriation acts through claims against state-linked entities).

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that Title III’s sweeping liability for any “person” who “traffics” would be significantly blunted if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke FSIA immunity, suggesting Congress meant to open the courts. But as Justice Kagan’s “middle path” underscores—and as Amerada Hess and Verlinden require—a substantive cause of action does not itself supply jurisdiction or unmistakably abrogate the FSIA’s comprehensive immunity/default-and-exceptions scheme; Title III’s silence on §§ 1604–1607 and § 1330(a) is dispositive under our clear-statement cases. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Turkiye Halk Bankasi further reinforces that we do not treat later remedial statutes as impliedly reworking FSIA’s calibrated structure absent explicit text. A narrow holding that Title III operates where an FSIA exception is satisfied preserves statutory coherence and avoids the foreign-relations and reciprocity consequences that counsel against inferring an immunity-stripping rule Congress did not clearly enact.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Title III’s cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be significantly undercut if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke FSIA immunity, suggesting Congress must have meant to reach them. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, Amerada Hess and Verlinden treat the FSIA—through § 1330 and §§ 1604–1607—as the exclusive jurisdictional and immunity framework, and Title III contains no unmistakably clear text amending that scheme or adding a new exception. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Turkiye Halk Bankasi reinforces the same textual premise: we do not infer immunity-stripping or jurisdiction-conferring effects from remedial breadth or statutory purpose when Congress knows how to speak clearly. On an original public meaning and textualist approach, Title III supplies a merits rule that operates only when an existing FSIA exception independently permits suit; anything more would be an implied repeal inconsistent with the FSIA’s comprehensive design.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point—that Title III’s sweeping cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be gutted if Cuban instrumentalities retain FSIA immunity—amounts to a purpose-driven implied repeal, and our precedents do not permit that move in this foreign-relations-sensitive domain. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Verlinden and Amerada Hess treat the FSIA and § 1330 as the exclusive gateway for jurisdiction and immunity, and Title III’s silence on immunity or jurisdiction lacks the unmistakably clear statement needed to displace §§ 1604–1607. Justice Barrett’s invocation of Turkiye Halk Bankasi reinforces the methodological point: when Congress intends to alter sovereign-immunity rules, it does so explicitly, not by general liability language. Title III still has real work to do within the FSIA framework—operating wherever an existing FSIA exception applies—without creating the unpredictable diplomatic and reciprocity consequences that an implied immunity-stripping rule would invite.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest point remains that Title III’s broad coverage of “any person” trafficking in confiscated property would be seriously undercut if FSIA immunity shields Cuban instrumentalities, especially given the statute’s remedial aims for victims. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes via Amerada Hess and Verlinden, the FSIA is the exclusive gateway for jurisdiction and immunity over foreign states, and Title III’s silence on immunity or § 1330 channeling falls short of the “unmistakably clear” statement we require to displace that framework. Justice Kagan’s proposed middle path best addresses the practical concern without rewriting the jurisdictional scheme: Title III supplies a cause of action only where an FSIA exception independently permits suit, preserving access to justice where Congress has already authorized it. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Halkbank further reinforces that we do not infer FSIA displacement from remedial purpose alone, particularly in a foreign-relations-sensitive domain where Congress knows how to craft explicit exceptions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest petitioner argument remains that Title III’s broad liability for any “person” who “traffics” would be substantially gutted if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke FSIA, but that remedial breadth cannot do the work of an unmistakably clear immunity abrogation. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Verlinden and Amerada Hess is decisive for me: absent clear jurisdictional language or an amendment to §§ 1604–1607, we should not treat Title III as silently displacing the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Justice Barrett’s invocation of Halkbank reinforces the same structural point—Congress may create substantive liability without altering the sovereign-immunity framework, and we should not infer an FSIA carveout from purpose and general terms like “person.” The workable, coherence-preserving path is to read Title III as providing a cause of action that can be litigated when (and only when) an FSIA exception independently permits suit, leaving any broader Cuba-specific abrogation to Congress to state expressly.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Title III imposes liability on “any person” who “traffics,” and that phrase in ordinary usage can encompass Cuban instrumentalities—so reading FSIA immunity as intact may narrow Title III’s practical reach. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses (echoing Verlinden and Amerada Hess), FSIA and § 1330(a) provide the exclusive jurisdiction/immunity gateway for suits against foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities, and Title III contains no clear jurisdictional grant or unmistakable statement amending §§ 1604–1607 or adding an exception. Respect for Congress’s chosen immunity framework and the foreign-relations consequences of implied abrogation support requiring Title III plaintiffs to proceed through the FSIA’s exceptions rather than bypassing them.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FSIA establishes a comprehensive, presumptive immunity regime for foreign states and their agencies or instrumentalities, and this Court has repeatedly described it as the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction” over a foreign state absent a statutory exception. See Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434, 438–39 (1989); see also Republic of Austria v. Altmann, 541 U.S. 677, 699 (2004). Title III of the LIBERTAD Act creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but nothing in its text unmistakably amends the FSIA’s jurisdictional/immunity framework or supplies an express immunity-stripping rule for Cuban instrumentalities; reading it to silently override the FSIA would create administrability and foreign-relations problems Congress typically addresses with clear instructions. A workable, text-faithful middle path is to allow Title III claims to proceed where plaintiffs can satisfy an applicable FSIA exception, preserving statutory coherence while giving Title III meaningful effect when its predicates are met.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis” for both immunity and subject-matter jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, requiring a plaintiff to fit within an FSIA exception before any federal court may proceed. See 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a); Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434–38 (1989); Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488, 493 (1983). Title III of Helms-Burton creates a cause of action, but it does not speak with the clarity needed to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive jurisdictional and immunity framework, and we do not infer implied repeals in so sensitive an area touching foreign relations and separation of powers. Without an applicable FSIA exception, the courts lack jurisdiction over Cuban agencies and instrumentalities notwithstanding Title III’s remedial aims.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” in U.S. courts, and Congress must speak clearly if it means to displace that immunity framework. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434, 439 (1989). Title III of Helms-Burton creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not expressly amend the FSIA or unmistakably abrogate the immunity of Cuba’s agencies and instrumentalities; reading it to do so would invite foreign-relations and workability problems by implying repeal rather than applying the settled FSIA structure. Consistent with judicial restraint and precedent, a Title III plaintiff must therefore establish an applicable FSIA exception under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604–1607 before the court may exercise jurisdiction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSIA establishes the presumptive immunity of foreign states and their agencies and instrumentalities and, as this Court has repeatedly said, supplies the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” in federal court absent an applicable FSIA exception. Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488 (1983); see also Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 443 (1989); Turkiye Halk Bankasi A.S. v. United States, 598 U.S. 264, 272 (2023). Title III of Helms-Burton creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082, but it does not contain a clear textual statement displacing the FSIA’s immunity framework or adding a new exception, and we do not infer abrogation of foreign sovereign immunity from statutory purpose alone. Because jurisdiction over a “foreign state” (including its instrumentalities) requires an FSIA exception, a Title III plaintiff must satisfy the FSIA to proceed against Cuban state agencies/instrumentalities.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FSIA establishes a comprehensive, exclusive framework for both immunity and federal-court jurisdiction over foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities, supplying the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction” absent a statutory exception. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434–35 (1989); 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1603(a). Title III creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not speak with the clear, unmistakable text needed to displace the FSIA’s presumptive immunity regime or to provide an independent jurisdictional grant outside § 1330, and reading it to do so would invite significant foreign-relations friction and instability. A procedurally fair, pragmatic approach therefore requires plaintiffs suing Cuban instrumentalities to satisfy an applicable FSIA exception before proceeding on the merits of a Title III claim.
